extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, publishers, technologists, librarians, and institutions involved in scholarly communication and peer review
extracted.subtask_short: peer review in the AI era
extracted.subtask_description: Announcing and framing the 2025 Peer Review Week theme focused on how artificial intelligence affects the practice, policies, and values of scholarly peer review. The page outlines key question areas for discussion and community engagement across editors, reviewers, publishers, and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Boundaries and Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: What should authors, editors, and reviewers disclose regarding their use of AI tools? How do we define accountability?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on transparency obligations when AI is used in authoring, editing, or reviewing. Includes determining what must be declared (e.g., tool name, extent of use), who is accountable for outputs produced with AI, and policy design to ensure responsible disclosure. Ties to questions of attribution, provenance, and trustworthiness of AI-assisted content.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI Literacy and Reviewer Training
rubrics_metrics.description: What knowledge and skills do reviewers need to assess AI-generated content or to responsibly use AI tools themselves?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers the need for training programs, reviewer competencies, and educational resources so reviewers and editors can detect, evaluate, and responsibly apply AI tools. May include familiarity with AI limitations, bias modes, reproducibility concerns, and understanding AI/ML methods used within manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias, Fairness, and Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Can AI reduce human bias, or does it risk amplifying it? How do we make the process more auditable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses risks that AI systems may introduce or amplify bias in reviewer selection, manuscript assessment, or decision-making. Emphasizes designing auditable workflows, transparency about algorithms and data used, monitoring outcomes for disparate impacts, and mechanisms for redress and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human vs. Machine Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: What roles and decisions should remain uniquely human, and how do we protect those in a hybrid review environment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeks to delineate tasks appropriate for automation versus those that must retain human oversight (e.g., ethical judgments, contextual interpretation). Guidance includes preserving human values, editorial responsibility, and safeguards to ensure machine outputs do not supplant critical human decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Models of Peer Review
rubrics_metrics.description: From open and collaborative review to structured assessments and reproducibility audits, how might AI support new review models?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explores how AI can enable or reshape alternative review formats (open review, collaborative review platforms, structured checklists, reproducibility audits). Considerations include how to integrate AI to scale these models, preserve transparency, and maintain quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and Fairness in Reviewer Selection (manuscript triage & reviewer suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can AI improve the efficiency and fairness of reviewer selection and could this alleviate the growing burden on peer reviewers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers use of AI for manuscript triage, automated reviewer suggestions, and workload balancing. Guidance stresses designing algorithms that promote inclusivity (reduce bias), transparency about matching criteria, and evaluation of impacts on reviewer diversity and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated Quality Checks and AI-generated Reviews — Responsible Use
rubrics_metrics.description: From automated quality checks to AI-generated reviews, machine learning is increasingly influencing how peer review is conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers the deployment of automated checks (plagiarism, statistical anomalies, format checks) and the possibility of AI-generated review text. Emphasizes responsible application: defining limits of machine-generated feedback, requiring disclosure, validating automated outputs, and ensuring such tools augment rather than undermine human judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardrails for Fairness, Reproducibility, and Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: What guardrails must be in place to ensure fairness, reproducibility, and trust?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for policies, standards, and technical controls that protect equitable outcomes, reproducible assessments, and the integrity of scholarly evaluation. Examples include audit logs, reproducibility audits, standards for reporting AI involvement, and oversight mechanisms to maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing AI/ML Methods Used Within Research (assessing methodology and data integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: How should peer review evaluate the use (and misuse) of AI/ML in research, ensuring data quality, transparency, and trustworthy reporting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that peer review must adapt to scrutinize AI/ML methods themselves — not just LLM use in writing — including validation of algorithms, data provenance, reproducibility of results, and adequate reporting of AI/ML workflows. Encourages publisher and funder recommendations to strengthen methodological review and trust in AI-driven science.
